title: Too many columns: selecting and shrinking features
hook: Drop the useless, merge the similar, or compress many columns into a few.
inPlainWords: More columns are not always better. Extra columns add noise, slow training and invite memorizing. You can drop columns, combine ones that say the same thing, or compress many into a few summary columns.

useCase.title: The cancellation table grew to 400 columns
useCase.story: Engineers added every log field they could find, so the cancellation table now has 400 columns and only 20,000 customers. Training is slow, the model overfits, and managers cannot tell what matters.

approaches.name: Keep everything
approaches.what: Feed all columns to the model.
approaches.greatWhen: You have lots of data and a robust model.

approaches.name: Choose by domain knowledge
approaches.what: Experts pick the columns that make sense.
approaches.example: Keep tickets, visits and basket size. Drop internal debug fields.

approaches.name: Simple cleanup filters
approaches.what: Drop columns that are empty, constant or duplicated.
approaches.avoidWhen: It will not catch subtle noise.
approaches.example: Remove 90 columns that are always blank.

approaches.name: Model-based importance
approaches.what: Train a model and keep the columns it relies on most.
approaches.greatWhen: You want a fast, practical ranking.
approaches.avoidWhen: Columns are highly correlated, so importance is unstable.

approaches.name: Combine similar columns
approaches.what: Merge columns that say the same thing.
approaches.example: Combine 12 spend columns into total and average spend.

approaches.name: Compression (PCA-style summaries)
approaches.what: Turn many numeric columns into a few summary columns that keep most of the variation.
approaches.greatWhen: Many correlated numeric columns, or you want to visualize.
approaches.avoidWhen: You must explain individual columns to people.

challenge.question: Which plan best cuts the 400 columns without losing important signal?

options.text: Remove empty, constant and duplicate columns, use importance from training data and expert review to keep the useful ones, and confirm on an untouched exam
options.why: It cuts noise while keeping the signal, and the exam stays honest.
Can work with a strong model, but it is slower and harder to explain.

options.text: Drop half the columns at random
options.why: You might drop the strongest signals.

options.text: Compress to 5 summary columns and explain those to managers
options.why: Compact, but managers cannot read what a summary means.

bestCase.title: Clean up, rank on training data only, keep the useful ones
bestCase.example: Empty and duplicate columns drop 400 to 310. Experts remove debug fields. Importance from training rows keeps 40 columns. The exam score holds, training is ten times faster, and managers see the top drivers.

worstCase.title: Choosing columns with the exam set
worstCase.example: The team keeps the 30 columns that score best on the exam data, then reports that exam score. The exam helped choose the columns, so the score is inflated. Live results are much worse.

steps.label: Rank by importance
steps.goes: A model ranks columns using the training rows only.
steps.goesWrong: Columns are ranked using the exam rows too, so the exam leaks into the choice.

steps.label: Score once on the exam
steps.goes: An honest result on data never used for choosing.

takeaway: More columns are not better columns. Cut noise using training data only, and keep the final exam untouched.
